student_question: Using a demand and supply diagram explain how a subsidy paid to bicycle producers changes equilibrium price and quantity.
student_answer: The subsidy lowers unit production costs so supply increases. At the original price a surplus appears; price falls and equilibrium quantity rises.

student_question: Using a demand and supply diagram explain how a tax on disposable cups changes equilibrium price and quantity.
student_answer: The tax raises firms' unit costs and contracts supply. The resulting shortage at the old price raises the consumer price and lowers equilibrium quantity.

student_question: Using a demand and supply diagram explain how increased household incomes affect the market for a normal good.
Using a demand and supply diagram explain how lower input costs affect the market for reusable bottles.
student_answer: Lower input costs increase supply. Equilibrium price falls while quantity rises.

student_question: Using an AD/AS diagram explain the short-run effect of an economy-wide rise in energy costs.
student_answer: Higher energy costs reduce short-run aggregate supply. The average price level rises and real output falls.

student_question: Using a currency-market diagram explain how greater foreign demand for a country's exports can affect its floating exchange rate.
student_answer: Foreign buyers require more domestic currency to pay exporters. Currency demand rises and the currency appreciates.

student_question: Using a currency-market diagram explain how reduced overseas tourism spending in a country affects its floating currency.
student_answer: Visitors purchase less of the domestic currency. Demand for it falls and it depreciates.

student_question: An economy experiences rising prices. Using an AD/AS diagram explain one possible cause of inflation.
student_answer: Greater consumer confidence raises household spending and aggregate demand. The price level rises as firms expand output in the short run.

student_question: Using an externality diagram explain why unregulated noise pollution from factories can cause overproduction.
student_answer: Nearby households bear noise costs that factories do not pay. Marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost so market output exceeds socially efficient output.

student_question: Using a Lorenz curve diagram explain how income transfers targeted at low-income households can affect income inequality.
student_answer: Transfers increase the share of income received by poorer households. The Lorenz curve moves toward the equality line and income inequality falls.

student_question: Using a money-market diagram explain how an increase in the money supply affects the equilibrium interest rate when money demand is unchanged.
student_answer: The money-supply curve shifts right. The interest rate falls until the quantity of money demanded equals the greater supply.

student_question: Using an externality diagram explain why vaccination may be underconsumed without intervention.
student_answer: Vaccination protects other people as well as the recipient. Marginal social benefit exceeds marginal private benefit so market consumption is below the socially efficient quantity.

student_question: Using a PPC diagram explain the difference between bringing unemployed resources into use and increasing productive capacity.
student_answer: Employing idle resources moves production from inside the PPC toward it. Greater productive capacity shifts the PPC outward.

student_question: Using a poverty-cycle diagram explain how low household incomes can perpetuate low labour productivity.
student_answer: Low income limits spending on nutrition and health. Poor health lowers productivity and earnings which keeps income low.

student_question: Using a circular-flow diagram explain how additional investment by small firms may increase national income.
student_answer: Investment is an injection into the circular flow. Firms' spending becomes income for others and raises aggregate expenditure and output.

student_question: Using a cost and revenue diagram explain how a monopolist can earn abnormal profit at its profit-maximizing output.
student_answer: The firm selects output where MC equals MR and obtains the price from its demand curve. If average revenue exceeds average cost at that output it earns abnormal profit.

student_question: Paper 1 part (a): Explain how a fall in consumer confidence may create a recessionary gap.
student_answer: Lower confidence reduces consumption and aggregate demand. Short-run equilibrium real output falls below potential output as firms reduce production. Reduced labour demand creates cyclical unemployment. The size and persistence depend on other spending components and on wage and price adjustment.

student_question: Paper 2 part (g). Source: A fictional economy has unemployment of 8 percent and inflation of 1 percent. School buildings require repairs and public debt is 40 percent of GDP. Using this information evaluate increased government infrastructure spending.
student_answer: Repair spending could raise aggregate demand and employment when unemployment is high and inflation is low. Better school facilities may also improve human capital over time. Implementation delays limit the immediate effect and borrowing creates future servicing costs. The outcome depends on spare capacity and project quality; targeted repairs could be appropriate if they can start promptly and deliver lasting benefits.

student_question: Explain two reasons why a public good may be underprovided by private firms.
student_answer: Non-excludability allows people to benefit without paying so firms struggle to collect revenue. Non-rivalry means an additional user need not reduce others' consumption and the price that maximizes access may not cover the provider's costs.
